g.passage: Tell me about the trading post first, Aponi said, before I had even set down my bundle. So I told her. We stood on the stone bridge below the mesa in the spring of 1879, a year after my family had gone east, and I described my father's ledgers and the schoolmaster's squeaking boots until she laughed. Once, when we were nine, her brother had dared us both to walk the parapet; the summer before I left, the flood had taken him from beneath these same arches. Neither of us mentioned him. For two days we grazed our talk around the edges of one pasture, wandering wide to horses, to weather, to the price of wool. Whenever the water grew loud below us, she would point out a hawk, and I would look where she pointed, though I saw no hawk. On the third evening she pressed a smooth river stone into my palm without explaining it, and I carried it east in my coat. Shadows of the arches lay long across the dry wash, and somewhere up the slope a dog was bringing the sheep down.

g.passage: When Paloma handed me the ring of keys that morning, she bowed as if presenting a crown, and I laughed so hard I nearly dropped them. The salt-water pool behind the Dayton rec center had been hers for thirty summers; I was nineteen, her apprentice, and the aquatic park across town had just offered me twice her wage. I mentioned it while we skimmed leaves. Paloma asked whether they would give me a whistle with my name engraved on it, and maybe a manager younger than my sneakers. We traded jabs down the length of the deep end. Then, testing the water, she held the vial up to the light longer than she needed to. Her father's crew had poured these walls, she said. Every child on Fifth Street had learned to float in the shallow end, me included, and the drain still stuck each November in a way no manual explained. She did not ask me to stay. She only showed me, slowly, where to kick the grate. I set down the net. Across the water, light lay flat on the tiles, and a dragonfly kept touching the surface and lifting away.

g.passage: Hasan counted chairs. At every wedding we staffed in Thessaloniki that summer of 1872, he circled the hall twice before the guests came, tapping each chair back like a priest blessing pews, and I, newly hired, learned to time my yawns to the movement of his lips. That evening the count collapsed within minutes: cousins perched on window ledges, the musicians spilled down the stairs, and an aunt sat squarely on his tally board. I braced for thunder. None came. Hasan stood among the dancers with his hands loose at his sides, watching a boy asleep across two laps. Much later, as we folded linens, he mentioned that his father had once lost a post over a single guest left standing, and that he had counted chairs every night since, though no one had ever asked him to. Then he set his tally slate on my stack of napkins. Keep it or break it, Sadia, he said, and went to help the cooks. Out on the street, a cart wheel ground slowly over the wet stones.

g.passage: Four objects lived in Jomo's back room: a treadle machine, a headless dressmaker's dummy, a radio that caught one station, and the runner-up plate from the 1979 district chess final, which he had lost to me when I was twelve. For ten years I had let people call me brilliant for beating a grown man. That afternoon I sat on his cutting table while he hemmed a pair of trousers, and I asked, idly, why the plate stayed hidden behind the radio rather than on the shelf with his tailoring prizes. __He pinned the hem, unpinned it, and pinned it again in exactly the same place.__ Then he said my name, Kagiso, as if starting over, and spoke of other things: the price of wool, my father's cough that winter, how quiet our house had been while my father lay in the hospital. A girl, he said, should have one thing to be proud of that has nothing to do with sickrooms. He did not mention chess. I looked at the plate a long time, and then at his hands, which never misjudged a move on cloth. Below, a bus ground its gears at the corner of Moi Avenue.

g.passage: Ma'am, this was in the type case, said the boy who brings the paper stock, holding out my husband's brass composing stick, which I had hunted for since the funeral. I thanked him coldly and counted the sorts in the drawer after he left. Widows in the press rooms of Port of Spain learn quickly that condolence and pilfering often arrive in the same hands. Yet he came back the next day to ask whether the stick had been set to the width of the Gazette or the hymn sheets, since the measure seemed odd to him. Only my husband had ever noticed such a thing. I showed him. He set three crooked lines, found each error himself, and reset them without a word of excuse. My sister-in-law Pearl tells everyone that Hortense has adopted a stray, and I let her. These days the composing stick is never where I leave it, and I have stopped counting the drawer. On the windowsill, the morning's proofs dry beside a jar of his marbles.

g.passage: Thandiwe had kept the boarding house on Bree Street for twenty years, and Lindiwe had lodged in its back room for nearly as long, paying in coins or, when coins were scarce, in reed mats woven to a pattern her grandmother had carried down from the hills. One winter evening Thandiwe cleared the kitchen table, laid out a bundle of reeds, and sat down with her sleeves rolled. Teach me, she said, before the pattern goes to sleep in your hands. Lindiwe snorted, but she pulled up a chair, and by the light of the stove the first rows appeared, crooked and stubborn. g.passage: Anniversaries matter to me. Ten years after my first novel appeared, I wanted a dinner on the harbor, speeches, a printed card with both our names. Eulalio, who had carried my sentences into English through three books, wanted nothing. We argued on the stairwell of my lodging on the Cornish coast, I on the landing, he two steps below, the skylight rattling in the sea wind. I reminded him that reviewers had praised the music of the English pages, and that he had asked for his name to be printed small on the title page, then smaller. He said that was rather the point. His part, he told me, had always been a lamp in the next room: enough to read by, never meant to be looked at. I wanted to argue that lamps can be thanked. Instead I asked him to write the card himself, in whatever size he liked. Overhead, a gull walked the slate roof, its claws scraping at every step.

the blue scarf I knitted through a Lyon winter,

g.passage: Astrid distrusted new gates. For forty years she had kept the oak gate of the Bergen cemetery standing by replacing a single rotten slat each spring, so that hardly a board of the first gate remained, though no mourner could have said when it changed. Her apprentice, Anahera, wanted the gate's hundredth year marked by something people would notice: a carved arch, gilt letters, a ribbon for the mayor to cut. Astrid listened, then handed her a plane and one slat sawn from the same stand of oak her own teacher had used. Anahera grumbled through the planing. When she fitted the board, its grain ran almost seamlessly into the slat beside it, which bore a faint carpenter's mark she did not recognize. Astrid touched the mark and said it was older than either of them. That evening the gate swung shut behind the last visitors, and the hinges, oiled that morning, made no sound at all.
